entries.6dd25db0be9c5b6d94f56af7c7df69b398a2fe08: <div sID="gen18226" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="52" osisID="Jer.52" sID="Jer.52"/> <div eID="gen18226" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18227" type="x-p"/> History is the best expositor of prophecy; and therefore, for the better understanding of the prophecies of this book which relate to the destruction of Jerusalem and the kingdom of Judah, we are here furnished with an account of that sad event. It is much he same with the history we had <reference osisRef="2Kgs.24.1-2Kgs.25.30">2 Kings xxiv. and xxv.</reference>, and many of the particulars we had before in that book, but the matter is here repeated and put together, to give light to the book of the Lamentations, which follows next, and to serve as a key to it. That article in the close concerning the advancement of Jehoiachin in his captivity, which happened after Jeremiah's time, gives colour to the conjecture of those who suppose that this chapter was not written by Jeremiah himself, but by some man divinely inspired among those in captivity, for a constant memorandum to those who in Babylon preferred Jerusalem above their chief joy. In this chapter we have, I. The bad reign of Zedekiah, very bad in regard both of sin and of punishment, <reference osisRef="Jer.52.1-Jer.52.3">ver. 1-3</reference>. II. The besieging and taking of Jerusalem by the Chaldeans, <reference osisRef="Jer.52.4-Jer.52.7">ver. 4-7</reference>. III. The severe usage which Zedekiah and the princes met with, <reference osisRef="Jer.52.8-Jer.52.11">ver. 8-11</reference>. IV. The destruction of the temple and the city, <reference osisRef="Jer.52.12-Jer.52.14">ver. 12-14</reference>. V. The captivity of the people (<reference osisRef="Jer.52.15-Jer.52.16">ver. 15, 16</reference>) and the numbers of those that were carried away into captivity, <reference osisRef="Jer.52.28-Jer.52.30">ver. 28-30</reference>. VI. The carrying off of the plunder of the temple, <reference osisRef="Jer.52.17-Jer.52.23">ver. 17-23</reference>. VII. The slaughter of the priests, and some other great men, in cold blood, <reference osisRef="Jer.52.24-Jer.52.27">ver. 24-27</reference>. VIII. The better days which king Jehoiachin lived to see in the latter end of his time, after the death of Nebuchadnezzar, <reference osisRef="Jer.52.31-Jer.52.34">ver. 31-34</reference>.
entries.3a083bc1ddd2ca03befa31818e300d97d7f67d87: <div eID="gen18227" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Jerusalem Taken by Nebuchadnezzar. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 588.)</title> <div sID="gen18228" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Zedekiah <hi type="italic">was</hi> one and twenty years old when he began to reign, and he reigned eleven years in Jerusalem. And his mother's name <hi type="italic">was</hi> Hamutal the daughter of Jeremiah of Libnah. <hi type="super">2</hi> And he did <hi type="italic">that which was</hi> evil in the eyes of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , according to all that Jehoiakim had done. <hi type="super">3</hi> For through the anger of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> it came to pass in Jerusalem and Judah, till he had cast them out from his presence, that Zedekiah rebelled against the king of Babylon. <hi type="super">4</hi> And it came to pass in the ninth year of his reign, in the tenth month, in the tenth <hi type="italic">day</hi> of the month, <hi type="italic">that</hi> Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon came, he and all his army, against Jerusalem, and pitched against it, and built forts against it round about. <hi type="super">5</hi> So the city was besieged unto the eleventh year of king Zedekiah. <hi type="super">6</hi> And in the fourth month, in the ninth <hi type="italic">day</hi> of the month, the famine was sore in the city, so that there was no bread for the people of the land. <hi type="super">7</hi> Then the city was broken up, and all the men of war fled, and went forth out of the city by night by the way of the gate between the two walls, which <hi type="italic">was</hi> by the king's garden; (now the Chaldeans <hi type="italic">were</hi> by the city round about:) and they went by the way of the plain. <hi type="super">8</hi> But the army of the Chaldeans pursued after the king, and overtook Zedekiah in the plains of Jericho; and all his army was scattered from him. <hi type="super">9</hi> Then they took the king, and carried him up unto the king of Babylon to Riblah in the land of Hamath; where he gave judgment upon him. <hi type="super">10</hi> And the king of Babylon slew the sons of Zedekiah before his eyes: he slew also all the princes of Judah in Riblah. <hi type="super">11</hi> Then he put out the eyes of Zedekiah; and the king of Babylon bound him in chains, and carried him to Babylon, and put him in prison till the day of his death. <div eID="gen18228" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18229" type="x-p"/> This narrative begins no higher than the beginning of the reign of Zedekiah, though there were two captivities before, one in the fourth year of Jehoiakim, the other in the first of Jeconiah; but probably it was drawn up by some of those that were carried away with Zedekiah, as a reproach to themselves for imagining that they should not go into captivity after their brethren, with which hopes they had long flattered themselves. We have here, 1. God's just displeasure against Judah and Jerusalem for their sin, <reference osisRef="Jer.52.3">v. 3</reference>. His anger was against them to such a degree that he determined to <hi type="italic">cast them out from his presence,</hi> his favourable gracious presence, as a father, when he is extremely angry with an undutiful son, bids him get out of his presence, he expelled them from that good land that had such tokens of his presence in providential bounty and that holy city and temple that had such tokens of his presence in covenant-grace and love. Note, Those that are banished from God's ordinances have reason to complain that they are in some degree <hi type="italic">cast out of his presence;</hi> yet none are cast out from God's gracious presence but those that by sin have first thrown themselves out of it. This fruit of sin we should therefore deprecate above any thing, as David (<reference osisRef="Ps.51.11">Ps. li. 11</reference>), <hi type="italic">Cast me not away from thy presence.</hi> 2. Zedekiah's bad conduct and management, to which God left him, in displeasure against the people, and for which God punished him, in displeasure against him. Zedekiah had arrived at years of discretion when he came to the throne; he <hi type="italic">was twenty-one years old</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.52.1">v. 1</reference>); he was none of the worst of the kings (we never read of his idolatries), yet his character is that he <hi type="italic">did evil in the eyes of the Lord,</hi> for he did not do the good he should have done. But that evil deed of his which did in a special manner hasten this destruction was his <hi type="italic">rebelling against the king of Babylon,</hi> which was both his sin and his folly, and brought ruin upon his people, not only meritoriously, but efficiently. God was greatly displeased with him for his perfidious dealing with the king of Babylon (as we find, <reference osisRef="Ezek.17.15">Ezek. xvii. 15</reference>, &c.); and, because he was angry at Judah and Jerusalem, he put him into the hand of his own counsels, to do that foolish thing which proved fatal to him and his kingdom. 3. The possession which the Chaldeans at length gained of Jerusalem, after eighteen months' siege. They sat down before it, and blocked it up, in the ninth year of Zedekiah's reign, in the tenth month (<reference osisRef="Jer.52.4">v. 4</reference>), and made themselves masters of it in the <hi type="italic">eleventh year in the fourth month,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.52.6">v. 6</reference>. In remembrance of these two steps towards their ruin, while they were in captivity, they kept <hi type="italic">a fast in the fourth month, and a fast in the tenth</hi> (<reference osisRef="Zech.8.19">Zech. viii. 19</reference>): that in the <hi type="italic">fifth month</hi> was in remembrance of the burning of the temple, and that in the <hi type="italic">seventh</hi> of the murder of Gedaliah. We may easily imagine, or rather cannot imagine, what a sad time it was with Jerusalem, during this year and half that it was besieged, when all provisions were cut off from coming to them and they were ever and anon alarmed by the attacks of the enemy, and, being obstinately resolved to hold out to the last extremity, nothing remained but a <hi type="italic">certain fearful looking for of judgment.</hi> That which disabled them to hold out, and yet could not prevail with them to capitulate, was the <hi type="italic">famine in the city</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.52.6">v. 6</reference>); there was <hi type="italic">no bread for the people of the land,</hi> so that the soldiers could not make good their posts, but were rendered wholly unserviceable; and then no wonder that <hi type="italic">the city was broken up,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.52.7">v. 7</reference>. Walls, in such a case, will not hold out long without men, any more than men without walls; nor will both together stand people in any stead without God and his protection. 4. The inglorious retreat of the king and his mighty men. They got out of the city <hi type="italic">by night</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.52.7">v. 7</reference>) and made the best of their way, I know not whither, nor perhaps they themselves; but the king was overtaken by the pursuers <hi type="italic">in the plains of Jericho,</hi> his guards were dispersed, and all his army was <hi type="italic">scattered from him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.52.8">v. 8</reference>. His fright was not causeless, for there is no escaping the judgments of God; they will <hi type="italic">come upon the sinner,</hi> and will <hi type="italic">overtake him,</hi> let him flee where he will (<reference osisRef="Deut.28.15">Deut. xxviii. 15</reference>), and these judgments particularly that are here executed were there threatened, <reference osisRef="Deut.28.52-Deut.28.53">v. 52, 53</reference>, &c. 5. The sad doom passed upon Zedekiah by the king of Babylon, and immediately put in execution. He treated him as a rebel, <hi type="italic">gave judgment upon him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.52.9">v. 9</reference>. One cannot think of it without the utmost vexation and regret that a king, a king of Judah, a king of the house of David, should be arraigned as a criminal at the bar of this heathen king. But he <hi type="italic">humbled not himself before Jeremiah</hi> the prophet; therefore God thus humbled him. Pursuant to the sentence passed upon him by the haughty conqueror, <hi type="italic">his sons were slain before his eyes,</hi> and all <hi type="italic">the princes of Judah</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.52.10">v. 10</reference>); then <hi type="italic">his eyes were put out,</hi> and he was <hi type="italic">bound in chains,</hi> carried in triumph to Babylon; perhaps they made sport with him, as they did with Samson when his eyes were put out; however, he was condemned to perpetual imprisonment, wearing out the remainder of his life (I cannot say his days, for he saw day no more) in darkness and misery. He was kept in prison till <hi type="italic">the day of his death,</hi> but had some honour done him at his funeral, <reference osisRef="Jer.34.5">ch. xxxiv. 5</reference>. Jeremiah had often told him what it would come to, but he would not take warning when he might have prevented it.
entries.480f6076ca4136cd6d20e489ba762d9792fc23b4: <div eID="gen18229" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Babylonish Captivity. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 588.)</title> <div sID="gen18230" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">12</hi> Now in the fifth month, in the tenth <hi type="italic">day</hi> of the month, which <hi type="italic">was</hi> the nineteenth year of Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon, came Nebuzaradan, captain of the guard, <hi type="italic">which</hi> served the king of Babylon, into Jerusalem, <hi type="super">13</hi> And burned the house of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and the king's house; and all the houses of Jerusalem, and all the houses of the great <hi type="italic">men,</hi> burned he with fire: <hi type="super">14</hi> And all the army of the Chaldeans, that <hi type="italic">were</hi> with the captain of the guard, brake down all the walls of Jerusalem round about. <hi type="super">15</hi> Then Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard carried away captive <hi type="italic">certain</hi> of the poor of the people, and the residue of the people that remained in the city, and those that fell away, that fell to the king of Babylon, and the rest of the multitude. <hi type="super">16</hi> But Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard left <hi type="italic">certain</hi> of the poor of the land for vinedressers and for husbandmen. <hi type="super">17</hi> Also the pillars of brass that <hi type="italic">were</hi> in the house of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and the bases, and the brasen sea that <hi type="italic">was</hi> in the house of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , the Chaldeans brake, and carried all the brass of them to Babylon. <hi type="super">18</hi> The caldrons also, and the shovels, and the snuffers, and the bowls, and the spoons, and all the vessels of brass wherewith they ministered, took they away. <hi type="super">19</hi> And the basons, and the firepans, and the bowls, and the caldrons, and the candlesticks, and the spoons, and the cups; <hi type="italic">that</hi> which <hi type="italic">was</hi> of gold <hi type="italic">in</hi> gold, and <hi type="italic">that</hi> which <hi type="italic">was</hi> of silver <hi type="italic">in</hi> silver, took the captain of the guard away. <hi type="super">20</hi> The two pillars, one sea, and twelve brasen bulls that <hi type="italic">were</hi> under the bases, which king Solomon had made in the house of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : the brass of all these vessels was without weight. <hi type="super">21</hi> And <hi type="italic">concerning</hi> the pillars, the height of one pillar <hi type="italic">was</hi> eighteen cubits; and a fillet of twelve cubits did compass it; and the thickness thereof <hi type="italic">was</hi> four fingers: <hi type="italic">it was</hi> hollow. <hi type="super">22</hi> And a chapiter of brass <hi type="italic">was</hi> upon it; and the height of one chapiter <hi type="italic">was</hi> five cubits, with network and pomegranates upon the chapiters round about, all <hi type="italic">of</hi> brass. The second pillar also and the pomegranates <hi type="italic">were</hi> like unto these. <hi type="super">23</hi> And there were ninety and six pomegranates on a side; <hi type="italic">and</hi> all the pomegranates upon the network <hi type="italic">were</hi> a hundred round about. <div eID="gen18230" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18231" type="x-p"/> We have here an account of the woeful havoc that was made by the Chaldean army, a month after the city was taken, under the command of Nebuzaradan, who was <hi type="italic">captain of the guard,</hi> or general of the army, in this action. In the margin he is called the <hi type="italic">chief of the slaughter-men,</hi> or <hi type="italic">executioners;</hi> for soldiers are but slaughter-men, and God employs them as executioners of his sentence against a sinful people. Nebuzaradan was chief of those soldiers, but, in the execution he did, we have reason to fear he had no eye to God, but he served the king of Babylon and his own designs, now that he came into Jerusalem, into the very bowels of it, as captain of the slaughter-men there. And, 1. He laid the temple in ashes, having first plundered it of every thing that was valuable: He <hi type="italic">burnt the house of the Lord,</hi> that holy and beautiful house, where their <hi type="italic">fathers praised him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.64.11">Isa. lxiv. 11</reference>. 2. He burnt the royal palace, probably that which Solomon built after he had built the temple, which was, ever since, <hi type="italic">the king's house.</hi> 3. He burnt <hi type="italic">all the houses of Jerusalem,</hi> that is, all the houses of the great men, or those particularly; if any escaped, it was only some sorry cottages for the poor of the land. 4. He <hi type="italic">broke down all the walls of Jerusalem,</hi> to be revenged upon them for standing in the way of his army so long. Thus, of a defenced city, it was made a ruin, <reference osisRef="Isa.25.2">Isa. xxv. 2</reference>. 5. He <hi type="italic">carried away many into captivity</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.52.15">v. 15</reference>); he took away <hi type="italic">certain of the poor of the people,</hi> that is, of the people in the city, for <hi type="italic">the poor of the land</hi> (the poor of the country) he left for <hi type="italic">vine-dressers and husbandmen.</hi> He also carried off <hi type="italic">the residue of the people that remained in the city,</hi> that had escaped the sword and famine, and the deserters, such as he thought fit, or rather such as God thought fit; for he had already determined some for the <hi type="italic">pestilence,</hi> some for the <hi type="italic">sword,</hi> some for <hi type="italic">famine,</hi> and some for <hi type="italic">captivity,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.15.2">ch. xv. 2</reference>. But, 6. Nothing is more particularly and largely related here than the carrying away of the appurtenances of the temple. All that were of great value were carried away before, <hi type="italic">the vessels of silver and gold,</hi> yet some of that sort remained, which were now carried away, <reference osisRef="Jer.52.19">v. 19</reference>. But most of the temple-prey that was now seized was of brass, which, being of less value, was carried off last. When the gold was gone, the brass soon went after it, because the people repented not, according to Jeremiah's prediction, <reference osisRef="Jer.27.19">ch. xxvii. 19</reference>, &c. When the walls of the city were demolished, the pillars of the temple were pulled down too, and both in token that God, who was the strength and stay both of their civil and their ecclesiastical government, had departed from them. No walls can protect those, nor pillars sustain those, from whom God withdraws. These pillars of the temple were not for support (for there was nothing built upon them), but for ornament and significancy. They were called <hi type="italic">Jachin—He will establish;</hi> and <hi type="italic">Boaz—In him is strength;</hi> so that the breaking of these signified that God would no longer establish his house nor be the strength of it. These pillars are here very particularly described (<reference osisRef="Jer.52.21-Jer.52.23">v. 21-23</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.7.15">from 1 Kings vii. 15</reference>), that the extraordinary beauty and stateliness of them may affect us the more with the demolishing of them. All the vessels that belonged to the brazen altar were carried away; for the iniquity of Jerusalem, like that of Eli's house, was not to be purged by sacrifice or offering, <reference osisRef="1Sam.3.14">1 Sam. iii. 14</reference>. It is said (<reference osisRef="Jer.52.20">v. 20</reference>), <hi type="italic">The brass of all these vessels was without weight;</hi> so it was in the making of them (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.7.47">1 Kings vii. 47</reference>), <hi type="italic">the weight of the brass was not</hi> then <hi type="italic">found out</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Chr.4.18">2 Chron. iv. 18</reference>), and so it was in the destroying of them. Those that made great spoil of them did not stand to weigh them, as purchasers do, for, whatever they weighted, it was all their own.
entries.cac04e9660e7ebc36710770016cd863acb722779: <div eID="gen18231" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Babylonish Captivity. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 588.)</title> <div sID="gen18232" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">24</hi> And the captain of the guard took Seraiah the chief priest, and Zephaniah the second priest, and the three keepers of the door: <hi type="super">25</hi> He took also out of the city an eunuch, which had the charge of the men of war; and seven men of them that were near the king's person, which were found in the city; and the principal scribe of the host, who mustered the people of the land; and threescore men of the people of the land, that were found in the midst of the city. <hi type="super">26</hi> So Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard took them, and brought them to the king of Babylon to Riblah. <hi type="super">27</hi> And the king of Babylon smote them, and put them to death in Riblah in the land of Hamath. Thus Judah was carried away captive out of his own land. <hi type="super">28</hi> This <hi type="italic">is</hi> the people whom Nebuchadrezzar carried away captive: in the seventh year three thousand Jews and three and twenty: <hi type="super">29</hi> In the eighteenth year of Nebuchadrezzar he carried away captive from Jerusalem eight hundred thirty and two persons: <hi type="super">30</hi> In the three and twentieth year of Nebuchadrezzar Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard carried away captive of the Jews seven hundred forty and five persons: all the persons <hi type="italic">were</hi> four thousand and six hundred. <div eID="gen18232" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18233" type="x-p"/> We have here a very melancholy account, 1. Of the slaughter of some great men, in cold blood, at Riblah, seventy-two in number (according to the number of the elders of Israel, <reference osisRef="Num.11.24-Num.11.25">Num. xi. 24, 25</reference>), so they are computed, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.18-2Kgs.25.19">2 Kings xxv. 18, 19</reference>. We read there of five out of the temple, two out of the city, five out of the court, and sixty out of the country. The account here agrees with that, except in one article; there it is said that there were five, here there were seven, of those that were <hi type="italic">near the king,</hi> which Dr. Lightfoot reconciles thus, that he took away seven of those that were near the king, but two of them were Jeremiah himself and Ebed-melech, who were both discharged, as we have read before, so that there were only five of them put to death, and so the number was reduced to seventy-two, some of all ranks, for they had all corrupted their way; and it is probable that such were made examples of as had been most forward to excite and promote the rebellion against the king of Babylon. <hi type="italic">Seraiah the chief priest</hi> is put first, whose sacred character could not exempt him from this stroke; how should it, when he himself had profaned it by sin? Seraiah the prince was <hi type="italic">a quiet prince</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.51.59">ch. li. 59</reference>), but perhaps Seraiah the priest was not so, but unquiet and turbulent, by which he had made himself obnoxious to the king of Babylon. The leaders of this people had caused them to err, and now they are in a particular manner made monuments of divine justice. 2. Of the captivity of the rest. Come and see how <hi type="italic">Judah was carried away captive out of his own land</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.52.27">v. 27</reference>), and how it spued them out as it spued out the Canaanites that went before them, which God had told them it would certainly do if they trod in their steps and copied out their abominations, <reference osisRef="Lev.18.28">Lev. xviii. 28</reference>. Now here is an account, (1.) Of two captivities which we had an account of before, one in the seventh year of Nebuchadnezzar (the same with that which is said to be in his eighth year, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.24.12">2 Kings xxiv. 12</reference>), another in his eighteenth year, the same with that which is said (<reference osisRef="Jer.52.12">v. 12</reference>) to be in his nineteenth year. But the sums here are very small, in comparison with what we find expressed concerning the former (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.24.14">2 Kings xxiv. 14</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.24.16">16</reference>), when there were 18,000 carried captive, whereas here they are said to be 3023; they are also small in comparison with what we may reasonably suppose concerning the latter; for, when all the residue of the people were carried away (<reference osisRef="Jer.52.15">v. 15</reference>), one would think there should be more than 832 souls; therefore Dr. Lightfoot conjectures that, these accounts being joined to the story of the putting to death of the great men at Riblah, all that are here said to be carried away were <hi type="italic">put to death</hi> as rebels. (2.) Of a third captivity, not mentioned before, which was in the twenty-third year of Nebuchadnezzar, four years after the destruction of Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="Jer.52.30">v. 30</reference>): Then <hi type="italic">Nebuzaradan</hi> came, and <hi type="italic">carried away</hi> 745 Jews; it is probable that this was done in revenge of the murder of Gedaliah, which was another rebellion against the king of Babylon, and that those who were now taken were aiders and abetters of Ishmael in that murder, and were not only carried away, but put to death for it; yet this is uncertain. If this be the sum total of the captives (<hi type="italic">all the persons were</hi> 4600, <reference osisRef="Jer.52.30">v. 30</reference>), we may see how strangely they were reduced from what they had been, and may wonder as much how they came to be so numerous again as afterwards we find them; for it should seem that, as at first in Egypt, so again in Babylon, the Lord made them fruitful in the land of their affliction, and the more they were oppressed the more they multiplied. And the truth is, this people were often miracles both of judgment and mercy.
entries.45f8a82d957a469f37800ac3296824daa524046a: <div eID="gen18233" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Jehoiachin Favoured by Evil-merodach. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 588.)</title> <div sID="gen18234" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">31</hi> And it came to pass in the seven and thirtieth year of the captivity of Jehoiachin king of Judah, in the twelfth month, in the five and twentieth <hi type="italic">day</hi> of the month, <hi type="italic">that</hi> Evil-merodach king of Babylon in the <hi type="italic">first</hi> year of his reign lifted up the head of Jehoiachin king of Judah, and brought him forth out of prison, <hi type="super">32</hi> And spake kindly unto him, and set his throne above the throne of the kings that <hi type="italic">were</hi> with him in Babylon, <hi type="super">33</hi> And changed his prison garments: and he did continually eat bread before him all the days of his life. <hi type="super">34</hi> And <hi type="italic">for</hi> his diet, there was a continual diet given him of the king of Babylon, every day a portion until the day of his death, all the days of his life. <div eID="gen18234" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18235" type="x-p"/> This passage of story concerning the reviving which king Jehoiachin had in his bondage we had likewise before (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.27-2Kgs.25.30">2 Kings xxv. 27-30</reference>), only there it is said to be done on <hi type="italic">the twenty-seventh day of the twelfth month,</hi> here <hi type="italic">on the twenty-fifth;</hi> but in a thing of this nature two days make a very slight difference in the account. It is probable that the orders were given for his release on the twenty-fifth day, but that he was not presented to the king till the twenty-seventh. We may observe in this story, 1. That new lords make new laws. Nebuchadnezzar had long kept this unhappy prince in prison; and his son, though well-affected to the prisoner, could not procure him any favour, not one smile, from his father, any more than Jonathan could for David from his father; but, when the old peevish man was dead, his son countenanced Jehoiachin and made him a favourite. It is common for children to undo what their fathers have done; it were well if it were always as much for the better as this was. 2. That the world we live in is a changing world. Jehoiachin, in his beginning, fell from a throne into a prison, but here he is advanced again to a throne of state (<reference osisRef="Jer.52.32">v. 32</reference>), though not to a throne of power. As, before, the robes were changed into prison-garments, so now they were converted into robes again. Such chequer-work is this world; prosperity and adversity are set the one over-against the other, that we may learn to <hi type="italic">rejoice as though we rejoiced not and weep as though we wept not.</hi> 3. That, though the night of affliction be very long, yet we must not despair but that the day may dawn at last. Jehoiachin was thirty-seven years a prisoner, in confinement, in contempt, ever since he was eighteen years old, in which time we may suppose him so inured to captivity that he had forgotten the sweets of liberty; or, rather, that after so long an imprisonment it would be doubly welcome to him. Let those whose afflictions have been lengthened out encourage themselves with this instance; the vision will at the end speak comfortably, and therefore wait for it. <hi type="italic">Dum spiro spero—While there is life there is hope. Non si male nunc, et olim sic erit—Though now we suffer, we shall not always suffer.</hi> 4. That god can make his people to find favour in the eyes of those that are their oppressors, and unaccountably turn their hearts to pity them, according to that word ( <reference osisRef="Ps.106.46">Ps. cvi. 46</reference>), <hi type="italic">He made them to be pitied of all those that carried them captives.</hi> He can bring those that have spoken roughly to speak kindly, and those to feed his people that have fed upon them. Those therefore that are under oppression will find that it is not in vain to hope and quietly to <hi type="italic">wait for the salvation of the Lord. Therefore</hi> our times are in God's hand, because the hearts of all we deal with are so. 5. And now, upon the whole matter, comparing the prophecy and the history of this book together, we may learn, in general, (1.) That it is no new thing for churches and persons highly dignified to degenerate, and become very corrupt. (2.) That iniquity tends to the ruin of those that harbour it; and, if it be not repented of and forsaken, will certainly end in their ruin: (3.) That external professions and privileges will not only not amount to an excuse for sin and an exemption from ruin, but will be a very great aggravation of both. (4.) That no word of God shall fall to the ground, but the event will fully answer the prediction; and the unbelief of man shall not make God's threatenings, any more than his promises, of no effect. The justice and truth of God are here written in bloody characters, for the conviction or the confusion of all those that make a jest of his threatenings. Let them <hi type="italic">not be deceived, God is not mocked.</hi>  <chapter eID="Jer.52"/> <div eID="gen18235" type="x-p"/> <div canonical="true" eID="gen17137" osisID="Jer" type="book"/>

entries.d94c29ad0f73a277ac6d4c853b5ee20cef5ac9fe: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10765"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 52</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Jer.52.1-Jer.52.34">Jr 52:1-34</reference>. Written by Some Other than Jeremiah (Probably Ezra) AS AN Historical Supplement to the Previous Prophecies</title> <div sID="gen19283" type="x-p"/> (See on <reference osisRef="Jer.51.64">Jr 51:64</reference>). Jeremiah, having already (thirty-ninth and fortieth chapters) given the history in the proper place, was not likely to repeat it here. Its canonical authority as inspired is shown by its being in the Septuagint version. It contains the capture and burning of Jerusalem, &c., Zedekiah's punishment, and the better treatment of Jehoiachin under Evil-merodach, down to his death. These last events were probably subsequent to Jeremiah's time.<div eID="gen19283" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19284" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10765"/><hi type="bold">3. through ... anger of ... Lord ... Zedekiah rebelled--</hi>His "anger" against Jerusalem, determining Him to "cast out" His people "from His presence" heretofore manifested there, led Him to permit Zedekiah to rebel (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.26">2Ki 23:26</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.27">27</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Exod.9.12">Ex 9:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.10.1">10:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.9.18">Ro 9:18</reference>). That rebellion, being in violation of his oath "by God," was sure to bring down God's vengeance (<reference osisRef="2Chr.36.13">2Ch 36:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.17.15">Eze 17:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.16.18">16, 18</reference>). <div eID="gen19284" type="x-p"/>
entries.691367b7d202c04270aeebd9786e27f81c561e32: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10766"/><div sID="gen19285" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10766"/><hi type="bold">4. forts--</hi>rather, towers of wood [Kimchi], for watching the movements of the besieged from the height and annoying them with missiles. <div eID="gen19285" type="x-p"/>
entries.66a9cbe965fd843230e4cce339f67babf405cc7e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10767"/><div sID="gen19286" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10767"/>7. (See on <reference osisRef="Jer.39.4">Jr 39:4</reference>). <div eID="gen19286" type="x-p"/>
entries.54d67a1f43997edb1201a88fa3384ab57e28778c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10768"/><div sID="gen19287" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10768"/><hi type="bold">9. gave judgment upon him--</hi>as guilty of rebellion and perjury (<reference osisRef="Jer.52.3">Jr 52:3</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Ezek.23.24">Eze 23:24</reference>). <div eID="gen19287" type="x-p"/>
entries.a5642e16deb1309fa4e63a6c6d37ea8bdb3444b5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10769"/><div sID="gen19288" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10769"/>11. <reference osisRef="Ezek.12.13">Eze 12:13</reference>: "I will bring him to Babylon ... yet shall he not see it."<div eID="gen19288" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19289" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">prison--</hi>literally, "the house of visitations," or "punishments," that is, where there was penal work enforced on the prisoners, such as grinding. Hence the Septuagint renders it "the house of the mill." So Samson, after his eyes were put out, "ground" in the Philistine prison-house (<reference osisRef="Judg.16.21">Jud 16:21</reference>). <div eID="gen19289" type="x-p"/>
entries.9250159f2b884da5929fa7f7637911622d90914a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10770"/><div sID="gen19290" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10770"/><hi type="bold">12. tenth day--</hi>But in <reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.8">2Ki 25:8</reference>, it is said "the seventh day." Nebuzara-dan started from Riblah on the "seventh" day and arrived in Jerusalem on the "tenth" day. Seeming discrepancies, when cleared up, confirm the genuineness of Scripture; for they show there was no collusion between the writers; as in all God's works there is latent harmony under outward varieties. <div eID="gen19290" type="x-p"/>
entries.b3bf1d1391a2739ad5f3b159570bd3500ea819fa: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10771"/><div sID="gen19291" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10771"/><hi type="bold">13. all the houses ... and all the houses of the great--</hi>the "and" defines what houses especially are meant, namely, the houses of the great men. <div eID="gen19291" type="x-p"/>
entries.cb186393df1fba4729d58b374de97ae25f632a99: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10772"/><div sID="gen19292" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10772"/><hi type="bold">15. poor of ... people--</hi>added to the account in <reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.11">2Ki 25:11</reference>. "The poor of the people" are of the city, as distinguished from "the poor of the land," that is, of the country. <div eID="gen19292" type="x-p"/>
entries.f05eabc6028e1a3ae86766787ce5bdf5a4591ac7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10773"/><div sID="gen19293" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10773"/><hi type="bold">17. brake--</hi>that they might be more portable. Fulfilling the prophecy (<reference osisRef="Jer.27.19">Jr 27:19</reference>). See <reference osisRef="1Kgs.7.15">1Ki 7:15</reference>, 23, 27, 50. Nothing is so particularly related here as the carrying away of the articles in the temple. The remembrance of their beauty and preciousness heightens the bitterness of their loss and the evil of sin which caused it.<div eID="gen19293" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19294" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">brass ... brazen--</hi>rather "copper ... of copper." <div eID="gen19294" type="x-p"/>
entries.df8c89b54cd4366d2b01e8bfa794cc4f7f62ebcd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10774"/><div sID="gen19295" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10774"/>18. (<reference osisRef="Exod.27.3">Ex 27:3</reference>). <div eID="gen19295" type="x-p"/>
entries.b3fe7595deab8d3202b50b81a0dbc8ab5861e9f6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10775"/><div sID="gen19296" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10775"/><hi type="bold">19. of gold in gold--</hi>implying that the articles were of solid gold and silver respectively, not of a different metal inside, or alloyed [Grotius]. Whole: not breaking them as was done to the "brass" (<reference osisRef="Jer.52.17">Jr 52:17</reference>). <div eID="gen19296" type="x-p"/>
entries.79daac213dce8e15d93840f21586c0b63474cbf6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10776"/><div sID="gen19297" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10776"/><hi type="bold">20. bulls ... under the bases--</hi>But the bulls were not "under the bases," but under the sea (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.7.25">1Ki 7:25</reference>, 27, 38); the ten bases were not under the sea, but under the ten lavers. In English Version, "bases," therefore, must mean the lower parts of the sea under which the bulls were. Rather, translate, "the bulls were in the place of (that is, 'by way of'; so the Hebrew, <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.9">1Sa 14:9</reference>), bases," or supports to the sea [Buxtorf]. So the Septuagint. <reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.16">2Ki 25:16</reference> omits the "bulls," and has "and the bases"; so Grotius here reads "the bulls (which were) under (the sea) and the bases." <div eID="gen19297" type="x-p"/>
entries.e648027b5be0d40c2de5ffa960ae5e2304766d0a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10777"/><div sID="gen19298" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10777"/><hi type="bold">21. eighteen cubits--</hi>but in <reference osisRef="2Chr.3.15">2Ch 3:15</reference>, it is "thirty-five cubits." The discrepancy is thus removed. Each pillar was eighteen common cubits. The two together, deducting the base, were thirty-five, as stated in <reference osisRef="2Chr.3.15">2Ch 3:15</reference> [Grotius]. Other ways (for example, by reference to the difference between the common and the sacred cubit) are proposed: though we are not able positively to decide now which is the true way, at least those proposed do show that the discrepancies are not irreconcilable. <div eID="gen19298" type="x-p"/>
entries.1e4bba1bd9675a3d6886966be270e8c925a3833f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10778"/><div sID="gen19299" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10778"/><hi type="bold">22. five cubits--</hi>so <reference osisRef="1Kgs.7.16">1Ki 7:16</reference>. But <reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.17">2Ki 25:17</reference> has "three cubits." There were two parts in the chapiter: the one lower and plain, of two cubits; the other, higher and curiously carved, of three cubits. The former is omitted in <reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.17">2Ki 25:17</reference>, as belonging to the shaft of the pillar; the latter alone is there mentioned. Here the whole chapiter of five cubits is referred to. <div eID="gen19299" type="x-p"/>
entries.10f43571d6e12aac418f2078975574afaca926ef: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10779"/><div sID="gen19300" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10779"/><hi type="bold">23. on a side--</hi>literally, (on the side) towards the air or wind, that is, the outside of the capitals of the pillars conspicuous to the eye, opposed to the four remaining pomegranates which were not seen from the outside. The pomegranates here are ninety-six; but in <reference osisRef="1Kgs.7.20">1Ki 7:20</reference> they are two hundred on each chapiter, and four hundred on the two (<reference osisRef="2Chr.4.13">2Ch 4:13</reference>). It seems there were two rows of them, one above the other, and in each row a hundred. They are here said to be ninety-six, but immediately following one hundred, and so in <reference osisRef="1Kgs.7.20">1Ki 7:20</reference>. Four seem to have been unseen to one looking from one point; and the ninety-six are only those that could be seen [Vatablus]; or, the four omitted here are those separating the four sides, one pomegranate at each point of separation (or at the four corners) between the four sides [Grotius]. <div eID="gen19300" type="x-p"/>
entries.6c7989be4d181912d1778ff36275b08d762f0d3a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10780"/><div sID="gen19301" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10780"/><hi type="bold">24. Seraiah--</hi>different from the Seraiah (<reference osisRef="Jer.51.59">Jr 51:59</reference>), son of Neriah; probably son of Azariah (<reference osisRef="1Chr.6.14">1Ch 6:14</reference>).<div eID="gen19301" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19302" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Zephaniah--</hi>son of Maaseiah (see on <reference osisRef="Jer.21.1">Jr 21:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.29.25">Jr 29:25</reference>). <div eID="gen19302" type="x-p"/>
entries.059e33de707af68867477480e666767325b4154b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10781"/><div sID="gen19303" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10781"/><hi type="bold">25. seven men--</hi>but in <reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.19">2Ki 25:19</reference> it is "five." Perhaps two were less illustrious persons and are therefore omitted.<div eID="gen19303" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19304" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">principal scribe of the host--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.33.18">Is 33:18</reference>). His office was to preside over the levy and enroll recruits. Rawlinson observes that the Assyrian records are free from the exaggerated expressions found in the Egyptian. A minute account was taken of the spoil. Two "scribes of the host" are seen in every bas-relief, writing down the various objects brought to them: the heads of the slain, the prisoners, cattle, sheep, &c. <div eID="gen19304" type="x-p"/>
entries.3a8259aa94f7af79559324e6aeddc3d093e6a1e0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10782"/><div sID="gen19305" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10782"/><hi type="bold">28. seventh year--</hi>in <reference osisRef="2Kgs.24.12">2Ki 24:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.14.16">14, 16</reference>, it is said "the eighth year" of Nebuchadnezzar. No doubt it was in part about the end of the seventh year, in part about the beginning of the eighth. Also in <reference osisRef="2Kgs.24.1-2Kgs.24.20">2Ki 24:1-20</reference>, ten thousand (<reference osisRef="Jer.52.14">Jr 52:14</reference>), and seven thousand men of might, and a thousand craftsmen (<reference osisRef="Jer.52.16">Jr 52:16</reference>), are said to have been carried away, But here three thousand twenty-three. Probably the latter three thousand twenty-three were of the tribe of Judah, the remaining seven thousand out of the ten thousand were of the other tribes, out of which many Israelites still had been left in the land. The thousand "craftsmen" were exclusive of the ten thousand, as appears, by comparing <reference osisRef="2Kgs.24.14">2Ki 24:14</reference> with <reference osisRef="Jer.52.16">Jr 52:16</reference>. Probably the three thousand twenty-three of Judah were first removed in the end of "the seventh year"; the seven thousand and a thousand craftsmen in the "eighth year." This was at the first captivity under Jehoiachin. <div eID="gen19305" type="x-p"/>
entries.ff9ee2847cf4e74469229f68ccb33c8910713c79: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10783"/><div sID="gen19306" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10783"/><hi type="bold">29. eighteenth year--</hi>when Jerusalem was taken. But in <reference osisRef="Jer.52.15">Jr 52:15</reference>, and <reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.8">2Ki 25:8</reference>, "the nineteenth year." Probably it was at the end of the eighteenth and the beginning of the nineteenth [Lyra].<div eID="gen19306" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19307" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">eight hundred and thirty and two--</hi>The most illustrious persons are meant, who no doubt were carried away first, at the end of the eighteenth year. <div eID="gen19307" type="x-p"/>
entries.a47726bcee3579af4ab71ce8c54c4ab9e2a38e42: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10784"/><div sID="gen19308" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10784"/>30. Not recorded in Kings or Chronicles. Probably it took place during the commotions that followed the death of Gedaliah (<reference osisRef="Jer.41.18">Jr 41:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.26">2Ki 25:26</reference>).<div eID="gen19308" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19309" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">four thousand and six hundred--</hi>The exact sum-total of the numbers specified here, namely, three thousand twenty-three, eight hundred thirty-two, seven hundred forty-five, not including the general multitude and the women and children (<reference osisRef="Jer.52.15">Jr 52:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.39.9">Jr 39:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.11">2Ki 25:11</reference>). <div eID="gen19309" type="x-p"/>
entries.184170401f956dbe2e5a4d2d67372e12eeb815a0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10785"/><div sID="gen19310" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10785"/>31. (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.27-2Kgs.25.30">2Ki 25:27-30</reference>).<div eID="gen19310" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19311" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">five and twentieth day--</hi>but in <reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.27">2Ki 25:27</reference>, it is "the twenty-seventh day." Probably on the twenty-fifth the decree for his elevation was given, and the preparations for it made by releasing him from prison; and on the twenty-seventh day it was carried into effect.<div eID="gen19311" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19312" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Evil-merodach--</hi>son and successor of Nebuchadnezzar [Lyra]; and the Hebrew writers say that during Nebuchadnezzar's exclusion from men among beasts, Evil-merodach administered the government. When Nebuchadnezzar at the end of seven years was restored, hearing of his son's misconduct and that he had exulted in his father's calamity, he threw him into prison, where the latter met Jeconiah and contracted a friendship with him, whence arose the favor which subsequently he showed him. God, in his elevation, rewarded his having surrendered to Nebuchadnezzar (compare <reference osisRef="Jer.38.17">Jr 38:17</reference> with <reference osisRef="2Kgs.24.12">2Ki 24:12</reference>).<div eID="gen19312" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19313" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">lifted up ... head--</hi>(Compare <reference osisRef="Gen.40.13">Ge 40:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.40.20">20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.3.3">Psa 3:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.27.6">27:6</reference>). <div eID="gen19313" type="x-p"/>
entries.264e73a352f29e793210609d3d4f09b53c80caa3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10786"/><div sID="gen19314" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10786"/><hi type="bold">32. set his throne above--</hi>a mark of respect.<div eID="gen19314" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19315" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the kings--</hi>The Hebrew text reads (the other) "kings." "The kings" is a Masoretic correction. <div eID="gen19315" type="x-p"/>
entries.6e932df99e0fa750eed4c0713d5b39c88abcb278: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10787"/><div sID="gen19316" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10787"/><hi type="bold">33. changed ... garments--</hi>gave him garments suitable to a king.<div eID="gen19316" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19317" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">did ... eat bread before him--</hi>(<reference osisRef="2Sam.9.13">2Sa 9:13</reference>). <div eID="gen19317" type="x-p"/>
entries.8690b2a6bbd0787050ed0504de92d5728e04a682: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10788"/><div sID="gen19318" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10788"/><hi type="bold">34. every day a portion--</hi>rather, "its portion," (compare <reference osisRef="1Kgs.8.59">1Ki 8:59</reference>, Margin). <chapter eID="Jer.52"/><div eID="gen19318" type="x-p"/> <div canonical="true" eID="gen16795" osisID="Jer" type="book"/>

entries.93e6d9c0dbb24edd337866261413f375e4513116: <div eID="gen30816" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen30817" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen30817" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30818" type="x-p"/> This chapter was added after Jeremiah's time probably by Ezra, after the return from the captivity, of which it gives a short account, nearly the same as in <reference osisRef="2Kgs.24.18-2Kgs.24.20">2Kgs 24:18-20</reference>, and <reference osisRef="2Kgs.24.18-2Kgs.24.20">2Kgs 24:18-20</reference>. It is very properly subjoined to the preceding prophecies, in order to show how exactly they were fulfilled. It likewise forms a proper introduction to the following Lamentations, as it gives an account of the mournful events which gave rise to them. Zedekiah's evil reign and rebellion against Nebuchadnezzar, <reference osisRef="Jer.52.1-Jer.52.3">Jer 52:1-3</reference>. Jerusalem is taken by the Chaldeans after a siege of eighteen months, <reference osisRef="Jer.52.4-Jer.52.7">Jer 52:4-7</reference>. Zedekiah pursued and taken in the plains of Jericho, and his whole army dispersed, <reference osisRef="Jer.52.8">Jer 52:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.52.9">Jer 52:9</reference>. The king's sons and all the princes of Judah slain in Riblah, <reference osisRef="Jer.52.10">Jer 52:10</reference>. Zedekiah has his eyes put out by order of the Chaldean monarch; and is afterward bound in chains, carried to Babylon, and imprisoned for life, <reference osisRef="Jer.52.11">Jer 52:11</reference>. Nebuzar-adan, the captain of the guard, burns and spoils the city and temple, <reference osisRef="Jer.52.12-Jer.52.19">Jer 52:12-19</reference>. The two pillars of the temple, with their dimensions and ornaments, <reference osisRef="Jer.52.20-Jer.52.23">Jer 52:20-23</reference>. The officers of the temple, and several others, carried away captives into Babylon, and then slain by order of Nebuchadnezzar, <reference osisRef="Jer.52.24-Jer.52.27">Jer 52:24-27</reference>. The number of Jews that Nebuchadnezzar carried away captive in the seventh year of his reign, <reference osisRef="Jer.52.28">Jer 52:28</reference>; in his eighteenth year, <reference osisRef="Jer.52.29">Jer 52:29</reference>; and in his twenty-third year, <reference osisRef="Jer.52.30">Jer 52:30</reference>. Evil-merodach, the son of Nebuchadnezzar, in the year of his accession to the throne of Babylon, (which was in the thirty-seventh year of the captivity, and the one hundred and ninety-first from the building of Rome, according to the computation of Varro), orders Jehoiachin to be taken out of prison, and treats him kindly for the remainder of his life, <reference osisRef="Jer.52.31-Jer.52.34">Jer 52:31-34</reference>. <div eID="gen30818" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30819" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen30819" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30820" type="x-p"/> Zedekiah was one and twenty years old - See <reference osisRef="2Kgs.24.18">2Kgs 24:18</reference>.
