entries.17ee95f673e30792032560c53502dee454694806: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen30834" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30835" type="x-p"/> The second priest - See the note on <reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.18">2Kgs 25:18</reference>. <div eID="gen30835" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30836" type="x-p"/> The three keepers - The priests who stood at the door to receive the offerings of the people, see <reference osisRef="2Kgs.20.9">2Kgs 20:9</reference>, and <reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.4">2Kgs 23:4</reference>.
entries.e4d6a696f91b812178a953c64b7a4f582e907652: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen30836" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30837" type="x-p"/> Seven men - that were near the king's person - These were privy counsellors.
entries.c18662c682ce33a9de692ae65a3c00660a15d2e1: <hi type="bold">Verse 28</hi> <div eID="gen30837" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30838" type="x-p"/> On these verses Dr. Blayney has some sensible remarks; I will extract the substance. These verses are not inserted in 2 Kings 25. Are we to conclude from these verses that the whole number of the Jews which Nebuchadnezzar, in all his expeditions, carried away, was no more than four thousand six hundred? This cannot be true; for he carried away more than twice that number at one time and this is expressly said to have been in the eighth year of his reign, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.24.12-2Kgs.24.16">2Kgs 24:12-16</reference>. Before that time he had carried off a number of captives from Jerusalem, in the first year of his reign, among whom were Daniel and his companions, <reference osisRef="Dan.1.3-Dan.1.6">Dan 1:3-6</reference>. These are confessedly not noticed here. And as the taking and burning of Jerusalem is in this very chapter said to have been in the fourth and fifth months of the nineteenth year of the reign of Nebuchadnezzar, those who were carried into captivity at the date of those events cannot possibly be the same with those that are said to be carried away either in the eighteenth or twenty-third year of that prince. Nor, indeed, is it credible that the number carried away at the time that the city was taken, and the whole country reduced, could be so few as eight hundred and thirty-two, (see <reference osisRef="Jer.52.29">Jer 52:29</reference>); supposing a mistake in the date of the year, which some are willing to do without sufficient grounds. <div eID="gen30838" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30839" type="x-p"/> Here then we have three deportations, and those the most considerable ones, in the first, in the eighth, and nineteenth years of Nebuchadnezzar, sufficiently distinguished from those in the seventh, eighteenth, and twenty-third years. So that it seems most reasonable to conclude with Abp. Usher, in Chronologia Sacra, that by the latter three the historian meant to point out deportations of a minor kind, not elsewhere noticed in direct terms in Scripture. <div eID="gen30839" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30840" type="x-p"/> The first of these, said to have been in the seventh year of Nebuchadnezzar, was one of those that had been picked up in several parts of Judah by the band of Chaldeans, Syrians, and others, whom the king of Babylon sent against the land previously to his own coming, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.24.2">2Kgs 24:2</reference>. <div eID="gen30840" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30841" type="x-p"/> That in the eighteenth year corresponds with the time when the Chaldean army broke off the siege before Jerusalem, and marched to meet the Egyptian army, at which time they might think it proper to send off the prisoners that were in camp, under a guard to Babylon. <div eID="gen30841" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30842" type="x-p"/> And the last, in the twenty-third year of Nebuchadnezzar, was when that monarch, being engaged in the siege of Tyre, sent off Nebuzaradan against the Moabites, Ammonites, and other neighboring nations, who at the same time carried away the gleanings of Jews that remained in their own land, amounting in all to no more than seven hundred and forty-five. <div eID="gen30842" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30843" type="x-p"/> Josephus speaks of this expedition against the Moabites and Ammonites, which he places in the twenty-third year or Nebuchadnezzar; but mentions nothing done in the land of Israel at that time. Only he says that after the conquest of those nations, Nebuchadnezzar carried his victorious arms against Egypt, which he in some measure reduced, and carried the Jews whom he found there captives to Babylon. But the Egyptian expedition was not till the twenty-seventh year of Jehoiachin's captivity, i.e., the thirty-fifth of Nebuchadnezzar, as may be collected from <reference osisRef="Eze.29.17">Eze 29:17</reference>; so that those who were carried away in the twenty-third year were not from Egypt, but were, as before observed, the few Jews that remained in the land of Judah.
entries.a5c5bc093d76e3e7829b50ea898aac487327edc6: <hi type="bold">Verse 31</hi> <div eID="gen30843" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30844" type="x-p"/> In the twelfth month - Answering nearly to our twenty-fifth of April, A.M. 3442. <div eID="gen30844" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30845" type="x-p"/> Lifted up the head of Jehoiachin - This phrase is taken from <reference osisRef="Gen.40.13">Gen 40:13</reference>. It is founded on the observation that those who are in sorrow hold down their heads, and when they are comforted, or the cause of their sorrow removed, they lift up their heads. The Hebrew phrase, lift up the head, signifies to comfort, cheer, make happy.
entries.98296c6b5d2d28661e052058bf024c4f444a45be: <hi type="bold">Verse 32</hi> <div eID="gen30845" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30846" type="x-p"/> Spake kindly - Conversed freely with him. <div eID="gen30846" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30847" type="x-p"/> Set his throne - Gave him a more respectable seat than any of the captive princes, or better than even his own princes had, probably near his person.
entries.61687c2cf8a2501d29c251aa8d9f379d334bac7e: <hi type="bold">Verse 33</hi> <div eID="gen30847" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30848" type="x-p"/> And changed his prison garments - That is, Jehoiachin changed his own garments, that he might be suited in that respect to the state of his elevation. Kings also, in token of favor, gave caftans or robes to those whom they wish to honor. <div eID="gen30848" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30849" type="x-p"/> And he did continually eat bread before him - Was a constant guest at the king's table.
entries.1ec6bb6afb366320893f78362789247f5157f124: <hi type="bold">Verse 34</hi> <div eID="gen30849" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30850" type="x-p"/> And - there was a continual diet given him - This was probably a ration allowed by the king for the support of Jehoiachin's household. For other particulars, see the note on <reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.30">2Kgs 25:30</reference>. <div eID="gen30850" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30851" type="x-p"/> All the days of his life - I believe these words have been by mistake added from the preceding verse. There, they are proper; here, they are tautological. They are wanting in the Septuagint and in the Arabic. <div eID="gen30851" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30852" type="x-p"/> The preceding words, עד יום מותו ad yom motho, "to the day of his death," are wanting in two of De Rossi's and one of Kennicott's MSS. <div eID="gen30852" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30853" type="x-p"/> Coverdale ends thus: - All the days of his life until he died. This is better than the common Version. <div eID="gen30853" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30854" type="x-p"/> Immediately after this verse my old MS. Bible adds the following words: And done is aftir that into caitifte is brougt Israel, and Jerusalem is bestroide, satte Jeremye the prophet weepund, and weiled with this lamentation Jerusalem; and with bitter inwit sighand and criand weilawai, seide. Then follows in red letters: Here beginneth the Lamentation of Jeremye, that is intitle Cenoth; with the sortynge out of Ebrue letters. <div eID="gen30854" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30855" type="x-p"/> Aleph: How sitteth aloon the city, etc. See something of a similar kind from other authorities, at the beginning of Lamentations. <div eID="gen30855" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30856" type="x-p"/> Masoretic notes <div eID="gen30856" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30857" type="x-p"/> Number of verses in this Book, 1365. <div eID="gen30857" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30858" type="x-p"/> Middle verse, <reference osisRef="Jer.28.11">Jer 28:11</reference>. <div eID="gen30858" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30859" type="x-p"/> Masoretic sections, 31.  <chapter eID="Jer.52"/> <div eID="gen30859" type="x-p"/> <div canonical="true" eID="gen29139" osisID="Jer" type="book"/>

entries.e005e4f8ee848b826817201d2efe8aa6020e6442: <reference osisRef="Jer.52.1-Jer.52.11">Jer 52:1-11</reference> <div eID="gen14514" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14515" type="x-p"/> Fate of King Zedekiah at the taking of Jerusalem; cf. 2Ki 24:18; 2Ki 25:7, and <reference osisRef="Jer.39.1">Jer 39:1</reference>-7. The statements regarding Zedekiah’s ascension and his government, <reference osisRef="Jer.52.1-Jer.52.3">Jer 52:1-3</reference>, agree word for word with 2Ki 24:18-20, even to the variation השׁליכו, <reference osisRef="Jer.52.3">Jer 52:3</reference>, for השׁליכו (Kings). The length of the siege of Jerusalem, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Jer.52.4-Jer.52.7">Jer 52:4-7</reference></hi>, and the flight, capture, and condemnation of King Zedekiah and the princes of Judah, <reference osisRef="Jer.52.7-Jer.52.11">Jer 52:7-11</reference>, not only agrees with 2Ki 25:1-7, but also with <reference osisRef="Jer.39.1-Jer.39.7">Jer 39:1-7</reference>, where it is merely the forcible entrance into the city by the Chaldeans that receives special detail; see on Jer 39:3. The variation ויּחנוּ, <reference osisRef="Jer.52.4">Jer 52:4</reference>, instead of ויּחן (2Ki 25:1), does not affect the sense. As to the account given of the flight, capture, and condemnation of the king, both Jer 39 and 2 Kings omit the notices given in <reference osisRef="Jer.52.10">Jer 52:10</reference>, "and also all the princes of Judah he caused to be slain (i.e., executed) at Riblah," and in <reference osisRef="Jer.52.11">Jer 52:11</reference>, "and he put him in the prison-house till the day of his death." בּית־הפּקדּות has been rendered οἰκία μυλῶνος by the lxx; on this fact Hitzig bases the opinion that the Hebrew words signify "the house of punishment," or "the house of correction," in which Zedekiah was obliged to turn the mill like other culprits, and as Samson was once obliged to do (Jdg 16:21). But this meaning of the words cannot be substantiated. פּקדּה means "oversight, mustering, or visitation (<hi type="italic">Heimsuchung</hi>), or vengeance," e.g., <reference osisRef="Isa.10.3">Isa 10:3</reference>, but not punishment (<hi type="italic">Strafe</hi>), and the plural, "watches" (<reference osisRef="Ezek.9.1">Eze 9:1</reference>) and "custody," Ezek. 54:11; hence the expression used here signifies "the house of custody," or "the house of the watches." The translation of the lxx can decide nothing against this, because their interpretation is based upon traditions which are themselves unfounded. Regarding this, Ewald well remarks (<hi type="italic">History of the People of Israel</hi>, iii. p. 748 of 2nd ed.): "That Zedekiah must have laboured at the mill, as is mentioned in later chronicles (see Aug. Mai, <hi type="italic">Scriptorum veterum nova collectio</hi>, t. i. P. 2, p. 6; cf. <hi type="italic">Chr. Sam</hi>. Ch. xlv.), is probably a mere inference from Lam 5:13."
entries.c626cf38b73813190eabb6014e6c28dae01a04ce: <reference osisRef="Jer.52.12-Jer.52.14">Jer 52:12-14</reference> <div eID="gen14515" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14516" type="x-p"/> The destruction of Jerusalem and of the temple, and the carrying away of the people, which are only very summarily stated in <reference osisRef="Jer.39.8-Jer.39.10">Jer 39:8-10</reference>, are here related in complete accordance with the account given in 2Ki 25:8-17. The deviations for the most part originated through the freedom exercised by the epitomizer in his work, or only when mistakes were made by later copyists. The text before us has some amplifications (especially the notices regarding the ornaments of the brazen pillars, <reference osisRef="Jer.52.23">Jer 52:23</reference>) which are found nowhere else in the Old Testament. The difference in date between <reference osisRef="Jer.52.12">Jer 52:12</reference> ("on the tenth of the month") and the passage in Kings ("on the <hi type="italic">seventh</hi> of the month") has arisen through one number having been mistaken for another in copying; it cannot now be decided which is correct; see on 2Ki 25:18. As to Nebuzaradan, see on Jer 39:13. Instead of עמד , is found עבד in 2Ki 25:8, which certainly is a simpler reading, but one having less appearance of being the original. The only strange point is the want of the relative אשׁר in plain prose before עמד, which is probably to be pointed עמד. בּירוּשׁלים, instead of ירוּשׁלים (Kings), is a pregnant expression for "he came into Jerusalem." - Jer 52:14. From the expression את־כּל־חומות, as given in <reference osisRef="Jer.52.14">Jer 52:14</reference>, "all" is omitted in Kings, as being not indispensable for the meaning.
entries.1935e7291c00faae2711bf030fc6e77ee35eb9b3: <reference osisRef="Jer.52.15-Jer.52.16">Jer 52:15-16</reference> <div eID="gen14516" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14517" type="x-p"/> The first words, "And of the poor of the people," are wanting in Kings, and have been brought here, through an error on the part of the copyist, from the beginning of the next verse; for "the poor of the people" are first treated of in <reference osisRef="Jer.52.16">Jer 52:16</reference>, where it is stated that Nebuzaradan left them in the land, while <reference osisRef="Jer.52.15">Jer 52:15</reference> treats of those who were carried away to Babylon. The word האמון, instead of ההמון (Kings), seems to have originated simply through the exchange of א for ה, and to mean, like the other, the multitude of people. Hitzig and Graf are of opinion that אמון here, as in <reference osisRef="Prov.8.30">Pro 8:30</reference>, means workmaster or artificer, and that האמון denotes the same persons (collectively) who are designated החרשׁ והמּסגּר in <reference osisRef="Prov.24.1">Pro 24:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.29.2">Pro 29:2</reference>, and 2Ki 24:14. But this view is opposed by the parallel passage, <reference osisRef="Jer.39.9">Jer 39:9</reference>, where the whole of this verse occurs, and יתר העם הנּשׁארים stands instead of יתר האמון. "The rest of the people of Jerusalem" are divided, by ואת־ואת, into those who went over to the Chaldeans, and the rest of the people who were taken prisoners by the Chaldeans at the capture of the city. The statement that both of these two classes of the population of Jerusalem were carried away to Babylon is so far limited by the further declaration, in <reference osisRef="Jer.52.16">Jer 52:16</reference>, that Nebuzaradan did not carry away every one, without exception, but let a portion of the humbler inhabitants of the country, who had no property, remain in the land, as vinedressers and husbandmen, that they might till the land. Instead of מדּלּות הארץ there occurs in Kings מדּלּת, and in <reference osisRef="Jer.39.10">Jer 39:10</reference>, more distinctly, מן העם הדּלּים, "some of the people, the humbler ones," who had no property of their own. דּלּה, pl. דּלּות, is an abstract noun, "poverty;" the singular is used collectively, hence the plural is here used to supply the deficiency. For יגבים, from יגב, to plough, there is found instead, in 2Ki 25:12, <hi type="italic">Kethib</hi> גּבים, from גּוּב, with the same meaning.
entries.e13074438db7d16b2e8ec5db9caa63441dbc251f: <reference osisRef="Jer.52.17-Jer.52.23">Jer 52:17-23</reference> <div eID="gen14517" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14518" type="x-p"/> The carrying away of the vessels of the temple is more fully stated than in 2Ki 25:13-17. The large brazen articles, the two pillars at the porch (cf. 1Ki 7:15.), the bases (1Ki 7:27.), and the brazen sea (1Ki 7:23.), which were too vast in their proportions to be easily carried away to Babylon, were broken to pieces by the Chaldeans, who carried off the brass of which they were made. אשׁר לבּית is more correct than אשׁר  (Kings), and "all their brass" is more precise than simply "their brass" (Kings). In the enumeration of the smaller brazen vessels used for the temple service, <reference osisRef="Jer.52.18">Jer 52:18</reference>, there is omitted, in 2 Kings, ואת־המּזרקות, "and the bowls" (used in sacrifice); this omission is perhaps due merely to an error in transcription. The enumeration of the gold and silver vessels in <reference osisRef="Jer.52.19">Jer 52:19</reference> has been much more abbreviated in 2Ki 25:15, where only "the fire-pans and the bowls" are mentioned, while in the text here, besides these there are named "the basons," then "the pots (Eng. vers. <hi type="italic">caldrons</hi>), and the candlesticks, and the pans (Eng. vers. <hi type="italic">spoons</hi>), and the cups." For particulars regarding these different vessels, see on 1Ki 7:40, 1Ki 7:45, 1Ki 7:50. In <reference osisRef="Jer.52.20">Jer 52:20</reference>, reference is made to the fact that the mass of metal in the vessels that were carried away was without weight. The same is stated in 2Ki 25:16, where, however, there is no mention of the twelve brazen bulls; while in the text of Jeremiah, אשׁר תּחת המּכנות is faulty, and we must read instead, אשׁר תּחתּיו והמּכנות. The assertion of Graf, in his commentary on this verse, and of Thenius on 2Ki 25:16, - that the notice regarding the twelve brazen bulls is incorrect, because these were then no longer in Jerusalem (27:19), but had previously been removed by Ahaz from under the brazen sea for Tiglath-pileser, - we have already, under 2Ki 16:17, shown to be erroneous. The apposition of כּל־הכּלים  to לנחשׁתּם explains the reference of the suffix. In <reference osisRef="Jer.52.21-Jer.52.23">Jer 52:21-23</reference>, the narrator, in order to call attention to the amount of art exhibited on the vessels destroyed by the Chaldeans, gives a brief description of the brazen pillars with their capitals. This description is much shortened in 2Ki 25:17, and contains notices completing that which is given of these works of art in 1 Kings 7. For details, see the passage referred to.
entries.f732bdd8b5a4fe5df2d49c462f27a860d01232a2: <reference osisRef="Jer.52.24-Jer.52.30">Jer 52:24-30</reference> <div eID="gen14518" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14519" type="x-p"/> The account given regarding the arrest of the chief officers of the temple and of the city, and concerning their transportation to Riblah, where Nebuchadnezzar caused them to be executed, agrees with 2Ki 25:18-21, except in some unimportant variations, which, however, do not alter the sense; the explanation has been already given in the commentary on that passage. In 2 Kings, the account of the appointment of Gedaliah as the governor of Judah, together with that of his assassination by Ishmael, which follows the narrative just referred to, is here omitted, because the matter has bee already more fully stated in the passage <reference osisRef="Jer.40.7">Jer 40:7</reference> on to <reference osisRef="Jer.43.7">Jer 43:7</reference>, and had no close connection with the object of the present chapter. Instead of this, there follows here, in <reference osisRef="Jer.52.28-Jer.52.30">Jer 52:28-30</reference> (as a continuation of the remark made, <reference osisRef="Jer.52.27">Jer 52:27</reference>, "Thus was Judah carried away captive out of his own land"), a calculation of the number of the Jews taken to Babylon at the three deportations: in the seventh year of Nebuchadnezzar, 3023 Jews; in the eighteenth year, 832 souls from Jerusalem; and in the twenty-third year, 745 souls, - in all, 4600 persons. The correctness of these data is vouched for by the exactness of the separate numbers, and the agreement of the sum with the individual items. In other respects, however, they present various difficulties. There is, first, the chronological discrepancy that the second deportation is here placed in the eighteenth year of Nebuchadnezzar, in contradiction with <reference osisRef="Jer.52.12">Jer 52:12</reference>, according to which, the deportation after the taking of Jerusalem occurred in the nineteenth year of Nebuchadnezzar; and 832 souls could not well be carried out of Jerusalem during the siege. This difference can be settled only by assuming that this list of deportations was derived from another source than the preceding notice regarding the destruction of Jerusalem, in which the years of Nebuchadnezzar’s reign were reckoned in some other way than elsewhere in Jeremiah and in the books of Kings, probably from the date of the actual commencement of his reign, which followed a year after he first appeared in Judah, from which his reign is dated elsewhere; see <hi type="italic">Comm. on Daniel</hi> at Dan 1:1. According to this mode of computation, the seventh year would correspond to the eighth of the common reckoning, and be the year in which Jehoiachin was carried away to Babylon, together with a large number of the people. But this does not agree with 3023, which is given as the number of those who were carried away; for, at that time, according to 2Ki 24:14, 2Ki 24:16, as many as 10,000 Jews, or, according to another view of these verses, even 18,000, were carried away to Babylon. This difference does not permit of being explained in any way. Ewald (<hi type="italic">History of the People of Israel</hi>, iii. p. 738) accordingly assumes that in <reference osisRef="Jer.52.28">Jer 52:28</reference>, after שׁבע, the word עשׂרה has been omitted, as in <reference osisRef="2Chr.36.9">2Ch 36:9</reference>, where the age of Jehoiachin is given; hence he thinks that, instead of "in the seventh," we must read "in the seventeenth year of Nebuchadnezzar." On such a view, the reference would be to a deportation which took place under Zedekiah, a year before the capture, or during the time of the siege of Jerusalem, and that, too, out of the country districts of Judah in contrast with Jerusalem, Jer 52:29. This supposition is favoured not merely by the small number of those who are said to have been carried away, but also by the context of the narrative, inasmuch as, in what precedes, it is only the capture of Jerusalem and the deportation of the people in Zedekiah’s time that is treated of. Nägelsbach has objected to this supposition, that it was not likely the great mass of the people would be carried away during the war, at a time when the approach of the Egyptian army (cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.37.5">Jer 37:5</reference>) was an object of dread. But the objection does not weaken the supposition, since the former rests on two presuppositions that are quite erroneous: viz., first, that the deportation took place before the defeat of the auxiliary army from Egypt, where as it may have followed that event; and secondly, that the Chaldeans, by keeping the hostile Jews in the country, might have been able to get some assistance against the Egyptian army, whereas, by removing the hostile population of Judah, they would but diminish the number of the enemies with which they had to contend. We therefore regard this conjecture as highly probable, because it is the means of settling all difficulties, and because we can thereby account for the small number of those who were carried away in the deportations during and after the destruction of Jerusalem. <div eID="gen14519" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14520" type="x-p"/> Regarding the third deportation, which was effected by Nebuzaradan (<reference osisRef="Jer.52.30">Jer 52:30</reference>) in the twenty-third, or, according to another reckoning, in the twenty-fourth year of Nebuchadnezzar, i.e., in the fifth year after the destruction of Jerusalem, we have no other information; for the statement of Josephus, <hi type="italic">Antt</hi>. x. 9. 7, that Nebuchadnezzar made war upon the Ammonites and Moabites in that year, has not been placed beyond a doubt, and is probably a mere inference from this verse, taken in connection with the prophecies in Jer 48 and 49. Yet there is nothing improbable in the statement, viewed by itself. For it must be borne in mind that, after the appointment of Gedaliah as governor, and the departure of the Chaldean hosts, many Jews, who had fled during the war, returned into the country. Hence, in spite of the fact that, after the murder of Gedaliah, a multitude of Jews, fearing the vengeance of the Chaldeans, fled to Egypt, many may have still remained in the country; and many other fugitives may not have returned till afterwards, and given occasion to the Chaldeans for removing other 745 disturbers of the peace to Babylon, four or five years after Jerusalem had been laid in ashes. This deportation may have taken place on the occasion of the subjugation of the Moabites, Ammonites, and Idumeans, or during the war with the Phoenicians, possibly because they had rendered assistance to these nations against the Chaldeans. These verses thus contain nothing to justify the assumption of M. von Niebuhr (<hi type="italic">Gesch. Assyr. und Babels</hi>, S. 58, note) and Nägelsbach, that they are a gloss. The paucity of those who were carried away is not to be attributed to a desire on the part of the writer of this inserted portion to represent the calamity as not so very terrible after all; nor is it due to the substitution of the number of the Levites for that of the entire people, - two wholly arbitrary assumptions: it is completely explained by a consideration of the historical circumstances. The best of the population of Judah had already been carried away, and Zedekiah and his counsellors must have said to themselves, when they rebelled against Nebuchadnezzar, that the latter would not spare this time; thus they must have defended themselves to the utmost, as is shown by the very fact that the siege of Jerusalem lasted eighteen months. In this manner, war, pestilence, and famine carried off a great number of the population of Jerusalem; so that, of men who were able-bodied and fit for war, and who could be carried into exile, not more than 4600 fell into the hands of the Chaldeans. During the war, also, many had concealed themselves in inaccessible places, while the lowest of the people were left behind in the country to cultivate the fields. Still more strange might appear the circumstance that the sum-total of those who were carried away to Babylon, viz., 10,000 with Jehoiachin, and 4600 under Zedekiah, - 14, 600 in all, - is evidently disproportionate to the number of those who returned to Jerusalem and Judah under Zerubbabel, which number is given in Ezr 2:64 at 42, 360, exclusive of men and maid servants. For this reason, Graf is of opinion that still later deportations may have taken place, of which no mention is made anywhere. This assumption, however, has little probability. On the other hand, we must consider these points: (1.) In the accounts given of those who were carried away, only full-grown and independent persons of the male sex are reckoned, while, along with fathers, both their wives and their children went into exile. (2.) Even so early as the first capture of Jerusalem in the fourth year of Jehoiakim, a number of prisoners of war, perhaps not inconsiderable, came to Babylon; these might unite with the thousands of their brethren who were carried thither at a later period. (3.) When the exiles had settled down in Babylon, and there found not only a means of livelihood, but even in many instances, as is clear from several intimations, attained to opulence as citizens, many, even of those who had been left in the country, may have gone to Babylon, in the hope of finding there greater prosperity than in Judah, now laid waste and depopulated by war. (4.) From the time when the 10,000 were carried away with Jehoiachin, in the year 599 b.c., till the return under Zerubbabel, 536 b.c., 63 years, i.e., nearly two generations, had passed, during which the exiles might largely increase in numbers. If we take all these elements into consideration, then, in the simple fact that the number of those who returned amounts to nearly three times the numbers of those given as having been carried away under Jehoiachin and Zedekiah, we cannot find such a difficulty as entitles us to doubt the correctness of the numbers handed down to us.
entries.b4312d7c41e4d22b01564d594c46b2dcacc68ed3: <reference osisRef="Jer.52.31-Jer.52.34">Jer 52:31-34</reference> <div eID="gen14520" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14521" type="x-p"/> The closing portion of this chapter, viz., the notice regarding the liberation of Jehoiachin from imprisonment, ad his elevation to royal honours by Evil-merodach after Nebuchadnezzar’s death, substantially agrees with the account given of that even in 2Ki 25:27-30. The difference of date, "on the twenty-fifth of the month" (<reference osisRef="Jer.52.31">Jer 52:31</reference>), and "on the twenty-seventh of the month" in 2 Kings, has arisen through the entrance of a clerical error into one text or the other. The few remaining variations of the two texts have no influence on the meaning. As to the fact itself, and its importance for the people languishing in exile, we may refer to the explanation given at 2Ki 25:27.  <chapter eID="Jer.52"/> <div eID="gen14521" type="x-p"/> <div canonical="true" eID="gen13725" osisID="Jer" type="book"/>

               <ns0:p n="23">23 And there were ninety and six pomegra<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nates on a side, <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> 
                  <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">See 1 Kin. 7.10.</ns0:note> all the pomegranates upon the net-work, <ns0:hi>were</ns0:hi> an hundred round about <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">There are some differences as to the measure of these Cha<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />piters betwixt 2 <ns0:hi>Kings</ns0:hi> 25.17. and this Text, here the height of them is made to be five Cubits, there it is said to be three Cubits, that which is said to resolve this difficulty is, That there were three parts in the Chapiter, the <ns0:hi>square,</ns0:hi> the <ns0:hi>belly,</ns0:hi> and the <ns0:hi>crown,</ns0:hi> and that this Text gives an account of the whole; but that Text 2 <ns0:hi>Kings</ns0:hi> 25.17. gives an account one<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly of the <ns0:hi>belly</ns0:hi> and the <ns0:hi>crown</ns0:hi> which were no more than three Cubits. The like difference there is betwixt this Text, and 1 <ns0:hi>Kings</ns0:hi> 7.20. and 2 <ns0:hi>Chron.</ns0:hi> 4.13. about the number of the <ns0:hi>Pomegranates.</ns0:hi> In the book of <ns0:hi>Kings</ns0:hi> it is said the Pomegranates were in number <ns0:hi>two hundred,</ns0:hi> 2 <ns0:hi>Chron.</ns0:hi> 4.13. they are said to have been <ns0:hi>four hundred.</ns0:hi> The meaning is, There were an hun<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dred in a row, in the two rows two hundred, in the four rows (two upon each pillar) four hundred. Some other difference also there is about the particular number of Pomegranates on a side, which are here said to be but ninety six, which make on the two sides but one hundred ninety two, on the four sides but three hundred eighty four, and comes up neither to the two hundred mentioned in the book of Kings, nor to the number of four hundred mentioned in the book of <ns0:hi>Chronicles.</ns0:hi> Vide the <ns0:hi>English Annotations,</ns0:hi> where the learned Author hath observ<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed that in the <ns0:hi>Hebrew,</ns0:hi> what we translate <ns0:hi>of a side,</ns0:hi> is word for word <ns0:hi>Wind-ward,</ns0:hi> that is, toward the four Winds, so as the <ns0:hi>square</ns0:hi> Table was <ns0:hi>square,</ns0:hi> and also the <ns0:hi>bases,</ns0:hi> and there were twenty four on each side which made ninety six in all, to which four being added one at each corner this made an hundred. But these are niceties a satisfaction in which is of no great concernment to us, unless to satisfie such as would make use of these little things to question the authority of the Scriptures, because of these seeming contradictions of how little concern<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ment so ever they be as to our Faith and Holiness.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="24">24 ¶ And the captain of the guard took So<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />raiah the chief priest, and Zephaniah the second priest, and the three keepers of the <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. <ns0:hi>threshold.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> door <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">See the notes on 2 <ns0:hi>Kings</ns0:hi> 25.18. where we have the same words. This <ns0:hi>Seraiah</ns0:hi> was not he mentioned <ns0:hi>chapter</ns0:hi> 51.59. but the son of <ns0:hi>Azariah,</ns0:hi> 1 <ns0:hi>Chron.</ns0:hi> 6.14. By the <ns0:hi>second Priest,</ns0:hi> Interpreters understand him that supplied the place of the High Priest in case he were sick, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> he that was sent by <ns0:hi>Zedekiah</ns0:hi> to the Prophet, <ns0:hi>chapter</ns0:hi> 21.1. and whom <ns0:hi>Shemaiah</ns0:hi> chode by his Letters <ns0:hi>chapter</ns0:hi> 29.25. for not setting <ns0:hi>Ieremiah</ns0:hi> in the Stocks. It is probable there were more keepers of the door, but the Captain of the Guard took onely three of the Principal.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="25">25 He took also out of the city, an eunuch, which had the charge of the men of war, and seven men of them that <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. <ns0:hi>saw the face of the king.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> were near the kings person which were found in the city, and the <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>the scribe of the captain of the host.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> principal scribe of the host, who mustered the people of the land, and threescore men of the people of the land, <ns0:hi>that were</ns0:hi> found in the midst of the city <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">See 2 <ns0:hi>Kings</ns0:hi> 25.19. onely there is mention but of <ns0:hi>five men,</ns0:hi> here there is mention of seven, but probably two of them were of less note.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="26">26 So Nebuzar-adan the captain of the guard took them, and brought them to the king of Babylon to Riblah.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="27">27 And the king of Babylon smote them, and put them to death in Riblah, in the land of Hamah. Thus Judah was carried away captive out of his own land <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">See 2 <ns0:hi>Kings</ns0:hi> 25.20, 21.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="28">28 This <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> the people whom Nebuchadrez<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />zar carried away captive; in the seventh year, three thousand Jewes and three and twenty <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">That is in the time of <ns0:hi>Iehoiachin,</ns0:hi> 2 <ns0:hi>Kings</ns0:hi> 24.12, 13, 14. here it is said to be in the seventh year, there in the eighth year, it might be in part of both. But there is a difference in the number of the captives which are here said to be 3023, and 2 <ns0:hi>Kings</ns0:hi> 24.14, 16. seven thousand, or eight. It is thought by some that the number here mentioned were such as properly belonged to <ns0:hi>Iudah,</ns0:hi> and the number mentioned 2 <ns0:hi>Kings</ns0:hi> 24. were the number of the Captives of <ns0:hi>Iudah</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Benjamin.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="29">29 In the eighteenth year of Nebuchadrezzar he carried away captive from Jerusalem eight hundred thirty and two <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. <ns0:hi>Souls.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> persons <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">That was the year when the City was broken up.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="30">30 In the three and twentieth year of Ne<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />buchadrezzar, Nebuzar-adan the captain of the guard carried away captive of the Jews seven hundred, forty and five persons: all the persons <ns0:hi>were</ns0:hi> four thousand and six hundred <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">Of this we read nothing in holy Writ, some judge it to have been upon occasion of <ns0:hi>Ishmaels</ns0:hi> killing <ns0:hi>Gedaliah,</ns0:hi> but this was four years after the taking of the City, and we are not certain what at this time brought again the <ns0:hi>Chaldean</ns0:hi> Forces.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="31">31 ¶ And it came to pass in the seven and

thirtieth year of the captivity of Jehoiachin king of Judah <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Iehoiachin</ns0:hi> began his reign at eighteen years of age, 2 <ns0:hi>Kings</ns0:hi> 24.8. and reigned but three Moneths, but that he yielded himself to the King of <ns0:hi>Babylon</ns0:hi> besieging him <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 12. in the eighth year of the King of <ns0:hi>Babylons</ns0:hi> Reign. He was a prisoner in <ns0:hi>Babylon</ns0:hi> (as appeareth by this Text) in which cir<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cumstances he continued (as appears from this Text) about thirty years; which was during the whole reign of <ns0:hi>Nebuchad<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rezzar,</ns0:hi> sometimes called <ns0:hi>Nebuchadnezzar,</ns0:hi> sometimes <ns0:hi>Nebuchado<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nosor, Evil-Merodach</ns0:hi> was son to this <ns0:hi>Nebuchadrezzar,</ns0:hi> who in the twelfth Moneth of that year, the 25th. day of the Moneth (saith this Text, but 2 <ns0:hi>Kings</ns0:hi> 25.27. it is the <ns0:hi>twenty seventh day,</ns0:hi> but that difference may easily be reconciled, the Penman of this part of Holy Writ, might count precisely from the day of his Fathers death, and the penman of the book of <ns0:hi>Kings</ns0:hi> from the time of the Coronation of <ns0:hi>Evil-Merodach,</ns0:hi> or when he openly shewed himself as King; or the one might reckon from the day that <ns0:hi>Evil Merodach</ns0:hi> decreed the thing, the other from the day when he put it in Execution).</ns0:note> in the twelfth moneth, in the five and twentieth <ns0:hi>day</ns0:hi> of the moneth <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Iehoiachin</ns0:hi> began his reign at eighteen years of age, 2 <ns0:hi>Kings</ns0:hi> 24.8. and reigned but three Moneths, but that he yielded himself to the King of <ns0:hi>Babylon</ns0:hi> besieging him <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 12. in the eighth year of the King of <ns0:hi>Babylons</ns0:hi> Reign. He was a prisoner in <ns0:hi>Babylon</ns0:hi> (as appeareth by this Text) in which cir<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cumstances he continued (as appears from this Text) about thirty years; which was during the whole reign of <ns0:hi>Nebuchad<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rezzar,</ns0:hi> sometimes called <ns0:hi>Nebuchadnezzar,</ns0:hi> sometimes <ns0:hi>Nebuchado<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nosor, Evil-Merodach</ns0:hi> was son to this <ns0:hi>Nebuchadrezzar,</ns0:hi> who in the twelfth Moneth of that year, the 25th. day of the Moneth (saith this Text, but 2 <ns0:hi>Kings</ns0:hi> 25.27. it is the <ns0:hi>twenty seventh day,</ns0:hi> but that difference may easily be reconciled, the Penman of this part of Holy Writ, might count precisely from the day of his Fathers death, and the penman of the book of <ns0:hi>Kings</ns0:hi> from the time of the Coronation of <ns0:hi>Evil-Merodach,</ns0:hi> or when he openly shewed himself as King; or the one might reckon from the day that <ns0:hi>Evil Merodach</ns0:hi> decreed the thing, the other from the day when he put it in Execution).</ns0:note>, <ns0:hi>that</ns0:hi> Evil-merodach king of Babylon, in the <ns0:hi>first</ns0:hi> year of his reign, lifted up the head of Jehoiachin king of Judah, and brought him forth out of prison <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Lifting up the head</ns0:hi> sig<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nifies in Scripture the altering of ones estate that is in Misery, <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 40.20. which is all that is here meant, for his bringing him out of <ns0:hi>Prison</ns0:hi> is mentioned in the next words. The Reason of this favour is variously guessed at. The Reverend Author of our <ns0:hi>English Annotations</ns0:hi> fancieth, that <ns0:hi>Evil-Merodach,</ns0:hi> might be much of the same Age with him, and that <ns0:hi>Iehojachin</ns0:hi> got into the Acquaintance of this <ns0:hi>Evil-Merodach,</ns0:hi> during his thirty years Captivity, who considering his long imprisonment, and that now there was no danger of his heading the <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> (whose City had now been destroyed twenty five years and upward) this Prince out of his Humanity might shew him this favour, nor are such things unusual in Nations upon their changes of Princes and Counsellors.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="32">32 And spake <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. <ns0:hi>good things with him.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> kindly unto him, and set his throne above the thrones of the kings that <ns0:hi>were</ns0:hi> with him in Babylon <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">The King of <ns0:hi>Babylon</ns0:hi> might have other Kings his Prisoners, his Father having been so great a Conqueror, or he might have other Kings his Subjects, that might reside at his Court, either out of a particular kindness he had to <ns0:hi>Iehojachin,</ns0:hi> or in regard of the Fame of <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Solomon,</ns0:hi> from whom <ns0:hi>Iehoiachin</ns0:hi> line<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ally descended, he might do him this Honour.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="33">33 And changed his prison-garments: and he did continually eat bread before him all the days of his life.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="34">34 And <ns0:hi>for</ns0:hi> his diet, there was a continual diet given him of the King of Babylon, <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. <ns0:hi>

                  </ns0:note> every day a portion, until the day of his death, all the dayes of his life <ns0:note n="w" place="bottom">He treated him like a Prince with a respect becoming his former state, took care both for his Habit and Diet, for his Habit, that it should be decent, such as became a person of his quality, though a Captive: for his Diet, that he should have it in his Court, thereby learning others that Humanity which becometh all men to treat others with that are fallen under their power; that Decency, which becometh them as men, and as men whose circumstances have been better; doing to others, as we would they should do unto us. Thus <ns0:hi>Iehoiachin</ns0:hi>'s Lot was different from that of his Father <ns0:hi>Iehoiachim,</ns0:hi> whose bo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dy was cast out as we heard before: as also from that of his Uncle <ns0:hi>Zedekiah,</ns0:hi> who did not onely dye in <ns0:hi>Babylon,</ns0:hi> but died a <ns0:hi>prisoner,</ns0:hi> his Nephew <ns0:hi>Iehoiachim</ns0:hi> died there, and a Captive, but not in durance. These four last verses are found also 2 <ns0:hi>Kings</ns0:hi> 25.27, 28, 29, 30. and being found here in a <ns0:hi>Narrative form,</ns0:hi> related as a piece of History relating a thing done: not in a <ns0:hi>prophetical stile,</ns0:hi> are an Argument (as was said before) that this whole Chapter, is no part of the Prophesie of <ns0:hi>Ieremiah,</ns0:hi> and probably not wrote by him, for he beginning his Prophesie in the thirteenth year of <ns0:hi>Iosiah,</ns0:hi> who reigned thirty one years, and continuing it three months during the reign of <ns0:hi>Iehoahaz,</ns0:hi> and eleven years during the reign of <ns0:hi>Iehoiachim,</ns0:hi> and three months during the reign of <ns0:hi>Jehoiachin</ns0:hi> (or <ns0:hi>Jeconiah</ns0:hi>) and eleven years during the reign of <ns0:hi>Zedekiah</ns0:hi>; and <ns0:hi>Je<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>oiachin,</ns0:hi> outliving the reign of <ns0:hi>Zedekiah</ns0:hi> twenty five years, it must needs be sixty five years and an half after the word of the Lord first came to <ns0:hi>Jeremiah</ns0:hi> be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fore the death of <ns0:hi>Jehoiachin</ns0:hi>; so as the Prophet if he lived to that time must be near an hundred years old, which is not pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bable. Here now endeth the History of the Kingdom of <ns0:hi>Judah</ns0:hi>: I shall onely note the severe judgment of God upon this people, whose Kingdom was made up of the two Tribes of <ns0:hi>Judah</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Benjamin,</ns0:hi> and half the Tribe of <ns0:hi>Manasseh.</ns0:hi> In the numbering of the persons belonging to these two Tribes, <ns0:hi>Numb.</ns0:hi> 1. (count<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing half of the number of the tribe of <ns0:hi>Manasseh</ns0:hi>) we find <ns0:hi>One hun<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dred twenty six thousand one hundred, Num.</ns0:hi> 26. we find of them <ns0:hi>One hundred forty eight thousand four hundred and fifty.</ns0:hi> Here <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 30. we find no more of them carried into Captivity, than <ns0:hi>four thousand and six hundred.</ns0:hi> From whence we may judge what a multitude of them were slain by the Sword or killed by the Famine and the Pestilence, though we make a great allowance for such as were left in the land to dress Vineyards, and to till the ground. It is a dreadful thing to fall into the hands of the living God, to <ns0:hi>mock his messengers, despise his words,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>misuse his Prophets, till there be no remedy,</ns0:hi> as this People did, 2 <ns0:hi>Chron.</ns0:hi> 36.16.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
